chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, raising it (marfu'), said: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said:
The intellect is a concealing veil, and virtue is a manifest beauty;
therefore conceal the defects of your character with your virtue, and fight your vain desires with your intellect — cordiality will become submissive to you and love will manifest for you.

key_terms.الْعَقْل: Intellect/reason — in Shia thought, aql is the greatest divine gift and the foundation of religious obligation and moral discernment
key_terms.الْفَضْل: Virtue/excellence/merit — here specifically meaning moral and spiritual excellence that beautifies one's outward conduct
key_terms.الْمَحَبَّة: Love — deeper, more enduring love that emerges as a fruit of virtuous and rational self-conduct
key_terms.الْمَوَدَّة: Cordiality/warm affection — a social love characterized by kinship and sincerity, distinct from mere romantic love
key_terms.الْهَوَى: Vain desires/passions — the lower self's inclinations that oppose reason and virtue; a recurring object of moral combat in Islamic ethics

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Ali say about using intellect and virtue to improve character?
ai.summary: Imam Ali (AS) presents a paired wisdom on the complementary roles of intellect ('aql) and virtue (fadl) in human character. Just as the intellect serves to veil and conceal moral shortcomings, virtue functions as a radiant outward beauty. The teaching exhorts the listener to actively deploy both: use virtue to mask one's moral flaws, and use reason to subdue one's base desires — with the promised result being genuine affection and love from others. This saying reflects the Shia ethical tradition's deep integration of rational self-governance with outward social conduct.
